planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring once soil can be worked; Amur chokecherry establishes quickly and tolerates harsh winters, exposed sites, and poor or alkaline soils better than most flowering cherries.

directions: Amur chokecherry is grown chiefly for its glossy, amber-to-coppery bark that peels and curls in thin papery sheets, giving the trunk striking winter interest much like paperbark maple. Dense clusters of small white flowers open along the branches in mid-spring with an almond-like fragrance, followed by pea-sized black cherries that are too bitter and astringent for people but are eaten readily by songbirds. Native to the Amur River region of northeastern China, Korea, and the Russian Far East, it is among the most cold-hardy ornamental cherries available and tolerates poor or alkaline soils, though it is relatively fast-growing and shorter-lived than many landscape trees. It is commonly planted as a specimen for winter bark interest or included in windbreak and shelterbelt plantings across the northern Great Plains and prairie provinces.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in early spring once soil is workable, giving the arching, densely thorned canes room to spread as the shrub matures.

directions: Rosa sericea is unusual among roses for its four-petaled white flowers, rather than the five petals typical of almost every other rose species, giving the abundant early-summer blooms a distinctive cross-like shape. Fine, fern-like pinnate foliage and densely thorned, arching canes give the shrub an airy texture quite different from typical garden roses, and small orange-red hips follow the flowers in autumn. Native to high-elevation forests and scrub of the Himalaya and western China, this species is the parent of the well-known form f. pteracantha, grown for its oversized, translucent, blood-red young thorns. Give it an open, sunny site with room to arch outward, since it blooms best on mature wood and resents hard, repeated pruning.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; because this wild-type species sets abundant viable seed when cross-pollinated with ornamental cultivars, check local regulations before planting, as some states now restrict its sale.

directions: Pyrus calleryana is the untamed wild-type species behind familiar ornamental selections such as 'Bradford' and 'Cleveland Select,' and unlike those thornless cultivated forms it typically develops stout thorns on its branches along with a more irregular, variable crown. Clusters of small white five-petaled flowers open before the leaves in early spring and carry a strong, unpleasant scent that many gardeners notice up close. Small, hard, brown-speckled pome fruits about the size of a marble follow in fall and are far too gritty and astringent for people, though birds eat them eagerly and scatter the seed widely. Because named ornamental cultivars cross-pollinate freely and set abundant fertile seed, Callery pear has become one of the most aggressive invasive woody plants of the eastern and midwestern United States, and planting it is now discouraged or restricted in a growing number of states.

subcategory: wild pear tree used as rootstock

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; birchleaf pear tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline soil far better than most pear species and is prized mainly as a vigorous, disease-resistant rootstock.

directions: Pyrus betulifolia is a vigorous, deep-rooted wild pear from northern China with small, rounded, birch-like leaves (the source of its common name) that emerge silvery and felted before maturing to glossy green. Clouds of small white flowers open in early spring, followed by tiny, hard, brown-speckled fruits that are gritty and of no culinary interest but are readily taken by birds. Its deep taproot and tolerance of heat, drought, and alkaline or poor soils have made it one of the most widely used rootstocks for grafted pear orchards, valued especially for its strong resistance to fire blight and pear decline. Grown as a free-standing tree rather than as rootstock, it makes a tough, low-maintenance shade tree with good drought tolerance once established.
